segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if you were raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Set your minds on the things above, not on the things on the earth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Christ, your life, is revealed, then you too will be revealed with him in glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So put to death the parts of you that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Because of these the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Among them you too once walked, when you were living in these things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now you too must lay it all aside: wrath, rage, malice, slander, foul language from your mouth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not lie to one another, since you have stripped off the old self with its practices

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where there is no Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all and in all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: bearing with one another and forgiving each other if anyone has a complaint against someone. Just as the Lord forgave you, so you too must forgive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And over all these put on love, which is the bond of completeness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the peace to which you were called in one body. And be thankful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let the word of Christ dwell among you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with gratitude in your hearts to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Husbands, love your wives and do not grow bitter toward them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they do not lose heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Slaves, obey your human masters in everything, not working only when watched, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whatever you do, work at it wholeheartedly, as for the Lord and not for people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are slaves of the Lord Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whoever does wrong will be paid back for the wrong done, and there is no favoritism.

notes.phrase: the parts of you that are on the earth
notes.traditional: your members which are upon the earth
notes.note: The Greek says literally “the members that are on the earth,” where “members” means limbs or body parts. The phrase “on the earth” repeats verse 2, and the list that follows shows that the “limbs” are a figure for the practices the body is used for. Many modern versions paraphrase as “what is earthly in you.”

Some important early manuscripts lack these words, and some editors think they were added by copyists from the parallel at Ephesians 5:6. SBLGNT prints them as original, and they are translated here. “Sons of disobedience” is a Semitic idiom for people characterized by disobedience.

The Greek pronoun can be masculine (“among whom,” the disobedient people of verse 6) or neuter (“in which,” the vices of verse 5). With the longer text of verse 6 the reference to people is the more natural one and avoids simply repeating “in these things” at the end of the verse. If the words in verse 6 are not original, the pronoun must refer to the vices.

The Greek is literally “the old human being,” and in verse 10 simply “the new.” Most modern translations render “old self” and “new self,” taking it of the individual’s former and renewed way of being. Some interpreters read it corporately, as the old humanity in Adam and the new humanity in Christ, which suits verse 11, where the “new” is a place in which ethnic and social divisions no longer exist.

“Barbarian” was the Greek term for anyone who did not speak Greek and so stood outside Greek culture. Scythians, peoples from north of the Black Sea, were proverbial in the Greek world as the most savage of barbarians. The list moves to the furthest extreme of what a Greek reader considered uncivilized.

“Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a person who is not self-assertive or harsh in dealing with others. “Gentleness” or “humility” is the mainstream modern rendering.

Manuscripts vary here between “the Lord,” “Christ,” and “God.” “The Lord” has strong early support and best explains the others, which look like attempts to specify who is meant. The King James Version follows manuscripts reading “Christ.”

The noun means completeness or maturity, the state of having reached the goal, not flawlessness. The phrase can mean the bond that produces completeness, the bond that holds the virtues together as a complete whole, or simply “the perfect bond.” Several modern versions paraphrase along the lines of “which binds everything together in perfect harmony.”

notes.phrase: teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs
notes.note: The Greek phrases can be grouped in more than one way. “In all wisdom” may go with “dwell” instead of with “teaching,” and the psalms, hymns, and songs may go with “singing” instead of with “teaching and admonishing.” The arrangement here follows the parallels at Colossians 1:28 and Ephesians 5:19. “Among you” could also be “in you,” and “with gratitude” could be “with grace.”

The Greek is literally “lords according to the flesh.” The word for a slave’s master is the same word translated “Lord” at the end of the verse and in verses 23–24. The passage plays on this throughout, setting the masters of the ordinary human sphere against the one Lord whom slaves and masters alike must answer to.

The verse is addressed to slaves, who ordinarily had no right to inherit; inheritance belonged to sons of the household. A first-century hearer would have noticed the reversal in promising slaves an inheritance from the Lord.

notes.phrase: You are slaves of the Lord Christ
notes.traditional: for ye serve the Lord Christ
notes.note: The Greek verb form can be a statement (“you serve”) or a command (“serve the Lord Christ”); both are grammatically possible, and translations divide. The verb is from the same root as “slaves” in verse 22, and the rendering here keeps that link visible.

candidates.reason: Translations vary between “slave,” “servant,” and “bondservant” across the New Testament, and the choice affects both the household codes and the figurative use for believers and apostles.
The word ranges from physical body to human sphere to sinful nature, and renderings such as “flesh,” “sinful nature,” “human,” and “earthly” need a consistent policy across the letters.
It recurs in vice lists and in the divorce sayings, and versions vary between “fornication,” “sexual immorality,” and “unchastity.”
It recurs in the household codes and in passages on civil authority, where “submit,” “be subject to,” and “be subordinate” carry noticeably different tones.
The figurative use for conduct is frequent in Paul and John, and translators divide between keeping “walk” and rendering “live,” which matters where the same sentence also has a verb meaning “live.”
